analysis.one_liner: Expands workers' rights to organize and strike, adds employer penalties, and lets workers sue over labor violations.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Murray with 33 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never left the Senate labor committee and received no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the nation's main private-sector labor law in workers' favor. It would make it harder to classify workers as independent contractors or supervisors outside the law, ban the permanent replacement of striking workers, create civil fines of up to $50,000 per violation (doubled for repeat violators) and personal liability for company officers, and let workers sue employers directly instead of waiting for the labor board. It would also override state right-to-work laws by letting unions collect fees from everyone they represent, ban forced arbitration of collective legal claims, and require large federal contractors to disclose their labor law violations before winning contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Private-sector workers who want to form a union or bargain collectively, workers who strike, gig and staffing workers who could be reclassified as employees, and unions — especially in states whose laws let workers skip paying for union representation they receive. The bill's own findings cite union members earning about 25 percent more than comparable non-union workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers trying to organize and bargain

how_it_helps.text: The bill would define nearly anyone performing service as an 'employee' unless they are truly free from employer control and run their own business, and it would narrow the definition of 'supervisor,' pulling more workers under the law's protections.
It would make it an unfair labor practice to permanently replace a worker who strikes, ending a practice courts have allowed.

If bargaining and mediation fail on a first contract, a three-person arbitration panel would set binding terms for at least two years, addressing the problem the bill cites of roughly half of new campaigns never producing an initial agreement.
Employers violating the law would face civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat violations within five years, and directors or officers could be personally fined.

Workers could bring their own federal lawsuits with back pay, front pay, consequential damages, double liquidated damages, and possible punitive damages, instead of relying solely on the National Labor Relations Board.
Labor board orders would take effect on issuance, with a $10,000 penalty for each violation of an order, rather than requiring the board to ask a court to enforce them.
The bill would let unions and employers agree to require all workers in a bargaining unit to pay representation fees, overriding state right-to-work laws.

It would void contracts that force employees to give up the right to join collective legal claims, and federal contractors could not force employees into arbitration of sexual harassment or discrimination claims without the worker's voluntary consent.
Companies bidding for federal contracts over $500,000 would have to disclose labor law violations from the prior three years, with updates every six months.
Federal contractors would have to give workers itemized pay statements covering hours, overtime, pay, and deductions.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the direct costs: new fines, damages, personal officer liability, mandatory bargaining outcomes, easier union elections, and disclosure duties. Gig platforms and staffing firms could be forced to reclassify contractors as employees. Consumers and taxpayers could absorb some costs through higher prices and an expanded labor board, for which the bill authorizes funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, especially anti-union firms and federal contractors

drawbacks.text: Employers would face fines up to $50,000 per violation ($100,000 for repeat violators), personal liability for directors and officers, and a new wave of private lawsuits — costs that some employers, particularly smaller ones, would struggle to absorb.

If bargaining and mediation fail on a first contract, a government-supervised arbitration panel would impose binding contract terms on both sides for at least two years, taking the final deal out of the parties' hands.

The bill would override state right-to-work laws, requiring workers who decline to join a union to pay representation fees anyway; opponents of fair-share arrangements argue workers should not be forced to fund a union, though the bill's own findings counter that unions must represent everyone in a unit whether or not they pay.
The bill would reissue a federal contractor disclosure rule that Congress had repealed by law in 2017, restoring reporting requirements that contractor groups had opposed as burdensome and punitive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are substantial: real penalties for firing union supporters, protection for strikers, a path to a first contract, and standing to sue. The costs fall on employers, which was the point — but the arbitration-of-first-contracts provision is genuinely heavy-handed, and the fee requirement in right-to-work states would force some unwilling workers to pay for representation they receive. The bill was a broad rewrite, and its compliance burden would land hardest on non-union employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate's labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never considered it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on June 13, 2018, joined by 33 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action was ever taken — no committee markup, no vote, no floor consideration — before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the bill's new penalties, easier union elections, reclassification risk, and a ban on permanently replacing strikers are better off because it never came to a vote. The workers and unions who backed it gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers facing the bill's new rules

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Lamar Alexander

against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never brought the bill up for consideration; it received no markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 34 senators in all, including the minority leader — with no Republican support, and the Republican-led committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill imposes civil fines up to $100,000 per violation, personal officer liability, private lawsuits, and a process that can certify a union without employer participation in representation proceedings. Employers' interest in weak labor enforcement runs directly against workers' interest in enforcing their rights.
The new employee definition uses a strict control-and-independent-business test, which could force reclassification of many contractors as employees with bargaining rights.

Easier elections, faster first contracts, protection for strikers, and the right to collect fair-share fees from all workers they represent would rebuild union membership and revenue. Union gains in this bill run alongside workers' gains.

Contractors over $500,000 would disclose three years of labor law violations and submit to biannual updates, with violations factored into contract responsibility decisions — a revived version of a rule Congress had repealed.
